relationship: parallel union of justice and devotion
rationale: Love of righteousness and sincere seeking of the Lord correspond to Micah's requirement to do justice and walk with God.

relationship: parallel rejection of testing God
rationale: Wisdom connects finding God with refusing to test Him; Deuteronomy expressly forbids putting the Lord to the test.

relationship: parallel moral separation from God
rationale: Crooked reasoning separates people from God here, while Isaiah describes offenses standing between the people and God.

relationship: internal parallel of wisdom's purity
rationale: Wisdom's refusal to inhabit an evil-devising soul corresponds to the later declaration that nothing defiled enters her pure outflow.

relationship: related wrongdoing against the holy Spirit
rationale: The spirit of discipline flees deceit and is put to shame when injustice comes upon it; Ephesians likewise places its warning against grieving the Holy Spirit beside the removal of malice and slander.

relationship: close heart-and-kidneys examination motif
rationale: Both passages portray God examining the heart and kidneys, grounding accountability in knowledge of a person's interior life.

relationship: parallel universal presence of God's Spirit
rationale: The Spirit filling the inhabited world corresponds to the psalm's inability to escape God's Spirit in heaven, Hades or the distant sea.

relationship: parallel accountability for speech
rationale: Unjust speech cannot escape convicting justice; Matthew similarly makes spoken words subject to accounting and condemnation.

relationship: related divine knowledge of thought and speech
rationale: The examination of deliberations and report of words correspond to God's knowledge of the psalmist's reasonings and tongue.

relationship: narrative example of heard grumbling
rationale: Wisdom says grumbling is not hidden; Numbers explicitly reports the Lord hearing the congregation's grumbling and their words in His ears.

relationship: parallel restraint of harmful speech
rationale: Restraint of slander and destructive utterance corresponds to the prohibition of rotten speech and the removal of slander.

relationship: parallel appeal to abandon death-bringing wrongdoing
rationale: Wisdom warns against drawing destruction through one's works; Ezekiel urges the people to cast away impieties and asks why they are dying.

relationship: close denial of delight in death
rationale: God's lack of delight in the destruction of the living corresponds to His declaration that He does not desire the dying person's death.

relationship: related goodness and sustenance of creation
rationale: Wisdom calls created things life-preserving; Genesis describes plants given as food and judges the whole creation very good, without making Wisdom's additional claims about Hades.

relationship: parallel association of righteousness with life
rationale: Wisdom's immortality of righteousness corresponds to life in the ways of righteousness, without treating the proverb as a full account of immortality.

relationship: close covenant-with-death motif
rationale: The ungodly make a covenant with death here; Isaiah exposes rulers who claim agreements with death and a covenant with Hades.

relationship: related mortal lament within different arguments
rationale: The ungodly begin with short, sorrowful life and irreversible death; Job's lament describes short-lived humanity and the dead lying asleep until heaven is no longer stitched together. Wisdom subsequently rejects the ungodly conclusion.

relationship: contrast concerning the human spirit's origin and end
rationale: The ungodly attribute existence to chance and reduce breath to smoke; Ecclesiastes instead describes the spirit as given by God and returning to Him.

relationship: contrast concerning the spirit after death
rationale: The ungodly predict dispersion into air, whereas Ecclesiastes says the spirit returns to God; the relation is a contrast, not agreement with the quoted speakers.

relationship: shared disappearing-cloud and lost-place imagery
rationale: The ungodly compare forgotten life to a vanishing cloud; Job likewise compares the dead to a cleared-away cloud whose former place no longer recognizes him.

relationship: shared shadow and bounded-life imagery
rationale: The quoted speakers describe a passing shadow and sealed allotted time; Job similarly depicts a fleeing shadow and a divinely fixed limit to life.

relationship: parallel condemned response to mortality
rationale: The ungodly urge present enjoyment after denying hope beyond death; Isaiah condemns the feast justified by the claim that tomorrow brings death.

relationship: parallel indulgence in wine
rationale: The ungodly resolve to fill themselves with costly wine; Isaiah condemns prolonged wine drinking that neglects the Lord's works.

relationship: parallel revelry claimed under approaching death
rationale: The speakers claim revelry as their portion in the argument begun with death; Isaiah's condemned revelers likewise make enjoyment their answer to impending death.

relationship: direct moral contrast over vulnerable people
rationale: The ungodly propose oppressing the poor and sparing no widow; Exodus forbids mistreating widows and pressing poor debtors.

relationship: contrast between might and righteous judgment
rationale: The speakers make strength their law and dismiss weakness; the psalm requires judges to vindicate and rescue the poor and needy instead.

relationship: parallel persecution of the righteous
rationale: The ungodly plot against the righteous critic; the psalm similarly describes sinners watching the righteous and drawing weapons against the upright.

relationship: related claim of divine parentage under hostility
rationale: The righteous person calls himself the Lord's child; John records Jesus calling God His Father amid murderous opposition. This is a thematic parallel, not an asserted identification of the speakers.

relationship: parallel hatred of a moral reprover
rationale: The righteous person's presence reproaches the plotters' thoughts; Amos describes hatred of one who reproves at the gates.

relationship: parallel separation of a righteous way of life
rationale: The righteous person's different paths correspond to the blessed person's refusal to walk in ungodly counsel and devotion to the Lord's law.

relationship: shared separation and divine-fatherhood motifs
rationale: Keeping away from impurities and calling God father correspond to the instruction to separate from uncleanness and the promise of God as Father.

relationship: parallel hostile test of a righteous person's claims
rationale: The plotters propose testing whether his words prove true; the mockers demand rescue as a test of belief in Jesus and His trust in God.

relationship: close sonship-and-rescue taunt
rationale: Both hostile speeches connect claimed divine sonship with the demand that God rescue the persecuted person.

relationship: related abusive testing of the persecuted
rationale: The proposed examination through insult and torture corresponds to the soldiers' mocking, spitting and striking of Jesus before crucifixion.

relationship: related shameful execution and expected divine care
rationale: The ungodly condemn a person whose claim of divine care they challenge; Matthew places the same rescue challenge around the crucified Jesus.

relationship: parallel moral blindness of understanding
rationale: Wickedness blinds the plotters here; Ephesians links darkened understanding and ignorance to hardness of heart and impure conduct.

relationship: internal contrast of denied and promised reward
rationale: The ungodly fail to recognize holiness's reward; the following account explicitly promises immortality, benefits and mercy to the faithful.

relationship: creation-image parallel
rationale: Wisdom's claim that humanity is God's image recalls Genesis's creation in God's image; Wisdom adds its explicit interpretation in terms of eternity and incorruption.

relationship: related deception-and-death narrative
rationale: Wisdom interprets death's entry through the devil's envy; Genesis supplies the serpent's deception and humanity's return to earth, without itself naming envy or the devil.

relationship: shared divine-hand security and life
rationale: The righteous souls are secure in God's hand; Jesus likewise promises life and declares that no one can snatch His people from His or the Father's hand.

relationship: parallel misunderstood death of the righteous
rationale: Foolish observers misread the righteous person's departure; Isaiah likewise says no one understands the removal of the righteous.

relationship: close righteous-death and peace parallel
rationale: Wisdom contrasts apparent destruction with peace; Isaiah describes the righteous person's burial in peace.

relationship: related hope of immortality beyond mortality
rationale: The righteous hope in immortality despite apparent punishment; Paul likewise anticipates mortality putting on immortality and death's defeat.

relationship: parallel beneficial divine discipline
rationale: A little discipline brings great benefits here; Hebrews describes God's discipline as beneficial and producing righteousness afterward.

relationship: close gold-furnace and divine-testing image
rationale: Wisdom likens God's testing to gold in a crucible; Proverbs similarly compares the testing of gold and silver to hearts chosen before the Lord.

relationship: parallel future radiance of the faithful
rationale: The righteous shine at their visitation; Daniel likewise depicts the understanding and faithful as heavenly lights and stars.

relationship: parallel judgment and kingdom of the holy ones
rationale: Wisdom promises the righteous judgment over nations under the Lord's reign; Daniel assigns judgment and everlasting kingship to the holy people.

relationship: parallel remaining in divine love
rationale: The faithful remain with God in love here; Jesus similarly calls His disciples to remain in His love through keeping His commandments.

relationship: parallel judgment according to unrighteous conduct
rationale: Wisdom connects punishment to ungodly reasoning and departure from righteousness; Romans contrasts reward for good with wrath upon those obeying injustice.

relationship: close rejection of wisdom and discipline
rationale: Wisdom calls the despiser of wisdom and discipline wretched; Proverbs identifies despising both as the behavior of the ungodly.

relationship: related reversal of barrenness
rationale: Wisdom promises fruit to the undefiled barren woman; Isaiah tells a barren woman to rejoice in abundant children, using the image for a restored community rather than an identical individual situation.

relationship: close faithful-eunuch and temple-inheritance parallel
rationale: Both promise faithful eunuchs an honored portion in God's house; Isaiah expressly adds an everlasting name better than sons and daughters.

relationship: parallel righteous fruit as life
rationale: The glorious fruit of good labor and unfailing root of understanding correspond to a tree of life growing from righteousness's fruit.

relationship: internal development of unfruitful unlawful offspring
rationale: The failure of offspring from an unlawful bed is developed in the following chapter's illegitimate shoots and useless fruit.

relationship: internal contrast between age and moral honor
rationale: Long life does not secure honor for the offspring described here; the next chapter explains honorable age through understanding and an unstained life rather than years.

relationship: explicit same-chapter contrast of hope after death
rationale: The offspring described here have no hope if they die quickly, in contrast to the righteous whose hope is full of immortality despite their apparent affliction.

relationship: internal elaboration of the unrighteous end
rationale: The harsh end of an unrighteous generation is elaborated as dishonor, anguish, lost remembrance and a reckoning of sins.

relationship: parallel enduring honor beyond children
rationale: Wisdom values childlessness with virtue through immortal remembrance; Isaiah promises faithful eunuchs an everlasting name better than sons and daughters.

relationship: shared contest and enduring-crown imagery
rationale: Virtue is pictured winning undefiled prizes and marching crowned; Paul likewise uses disciplined athletic competition for an incorruptible crown.

relationship: contrast of rooted righteous life and unstable ungodliness
rationale: Wisdom denies the ungodly a deep root; the psalm contrasts the righteous tree beside water with ungodly chaff carried away.

relationship: shared wind-driven instability of ungodliness
rationale: The insecure branches are uprooted by winds; the psalm similarly depicts ungodly people as chaff driven away by wind, with a different plant image.

relationship: parallel removal of fruitless growth
rationale: Wisdom's useless, broken branches correspond to the tree without good fruit being cut down; both use failed fruit to depict moral failure.

relationship: parallel righteous death as peaceful removal
rationale: Wisdom grants rest to the righteous who die early; Isaiah presents the righteous person's removal from injustice and burial in peace.

relationship: parallel denial that years guarantee worth
rationale: Wisdom denies that honorable age is measured by years; Elihu similarly denies that the long-lived necessarily possess wisdom or judgment.

relationship: parallel wisdom rather than years as maturity
rationale: Wisdom substitutes understanding and an unstained life for gray hair; Elihu locates instruction in God's breath rather than mere length of life.

relationship: close pleasing-God and transfer motif
rationale: The unnamed righteous person pleases God and is transferred, closely recalling Enoch's pleasing God and being transferred; the Wisdom verse itself does not name Enoch.

relationship: parallel removal from surrounding evil
rationale: Wisdom describes removal lest evil alter the righteous mind; Isaiah says the righteous man is taken from the presence of injustice.

relationship: parallel corrupting action of desire
rationale: Desire alters an innocent mind here; James describes desire enticing a person and giving birth to sin and death.

relationship: explicit same-chapter explanation of mature short life
rationale: A short life can fulfill long years because the earlier lines define honorable maturity by understanding and an unstained life rather than elapsed time.

relationship: close misunderstood removal of the righteous
rationale: Both describe the righteous person's removal from wickedness and observers who fail to understand or take it to heart.

relationship: internal recurrence of mercy for the chosen
rationale: This statement repeats the earlier assurance that grace and mercy belong to God's chosen, explaining the apparent loss of the righteous.

relationship: related exemplary condemnation at judgment
rationale: The righteous dead expose the living ungodly here; Matthew similarly presents earlier repentant or wisdom-seeking people rising to condemn a later generation.

relationship: parallel failure to understand a righteous person's end
rationale: Wisdom's observers do not understand God's purpose in the wise person's end; Isaiah likewise stresses the uncomprehended removal of the righteous.

relationship: close divine-laughter reversal
rationale: The Lord laughs at those who despise the righteous person's end; the psalm likewise portrays the Lord laughing at the sinner because his day is coming.

relationship: parallel destruction of the ungodly's remembrance
rationale: Wisdom joins the ungodly's destruction to vanished remembrance; the psalm likewise describes their erased name and destroyed memory.

relationship: parallel reckoning of all deeds
rationale: Lawless deeds confront their authors at examination here; Ecclesiastes likewise places every deed, even what was overlooked, under divine judgment.

relationship: parallel confidence of the righteous
rationale: The righteous person's bold stance before former tormentors corresponds to the proverb's righteous person being confident like a lion.

relationship: related reversal of persecutors' expectations
rationale: Those who afflicted the righteous are astonished at his salvation; Isaiah likewise anticipates shame for those who hate the people addressed by the Lord.

relationship: internal recognition of former error
rationale: The anguished repentance of the persecutors realizes the narrator's earlier verdict that their reasoning was astray and ignorant of God's reward.

relationship: internal reversal of contempt and shame
rationale: The former mockers recall their insulting verdict on the righteous person's life and end, reversing the earlier proposal to torture him and condemn him to shameful death.

relationship: internal vindication of disputed divine sonship
rationale: The persecutors now recognize the righteous person's portion among God's sons and saints after previously treating his claim to divine sonship as something to disprove.

relationship: parallel moral paths of light and darkness
rationale: The persecutors confess that righteousness's light did not shine upon their way; Proverbs contrasts the shining righteous path with the dark, stumbling way of the ungodly.

relationship: parallel lawless paths opposed to the righteous way
rationale: Their admission of traveling destructive paths corresponds to the prohibition of ungodly ways and the contrast between righteous light and ungodly darkness.

relationship: parallel exposure of wealth's inability to save
rationale: The persecutors question the benefit of boastful wealth; the rich fool's accumulated goods similarly fail to help when his life is demanded.

relationship: shared fleeting-shadow image
rationale: The vanished advantages of the ungodly pass like a shadow; Bildad likewise calls human life on earth a shadow, within a different argument about limited knowledge.

relationship: shared elusive path of a seagoing ship
rationale: Wisdom's ship leaves no discoverable wake; Proverbs names a seagoing ship's path among tracks the speaker cannot comprehend.

relationship: shared elusive aerial track
rationale: Wisdom describes a bird's vanished path through the air; Proverbs likewise names the tracks of a flying eagle among elusive things.

relationship: internal failure of the promised lasting mark
rationale: Those who planned to leave tokens of enjoyment everywhere now confess that they vanished without a sign of virtue; their proposed legacy is exposed as empty.

relationship: parallel wind-driven disappearance of ungodliness
rationale: The ungodly person's hope is wind-borne dust and dispersed smoke; the psalm similarly pictures the ungodly as chaff flung away by wind.

relationship: parallel enduring life under divine care
rationale: The righteous live forever under the Most High's care; Jesus likewise promises eternal life and security in His and the Father's hand.

relationship: close royal-crown and divine-hand imagery
rationale: The righteous receive a crown and diadem from the Lord's hand; Isaiah calls restored Zion a crown of beauty and royal diadem in God's hand, with a different bearer of the image.

relationship: parallel divine-warrior imagery
rationale: God takes zeal as armor and turns creation against enemies; Isaiah likewise depicts God clothing Himself for righteous vengeance and coming in wrath.

relationship: close breastplate-and-helmet imagery
rationale: Both clothe the divine warrior in righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet; Wisdom specifies unfeigned judgment, while Isaiah names salvation.

relationship: related martial representation of divine wrath
rationale: Wisdom turns stern wrath into a sword; Isaiah portrays vengeance as divine clothing and the Lord's anger as a violent river. The shared theme is armed judgment, not identical weaponry.

relationship: close lightning-and-arrows imagery
rationale: Wisdom's aimed lightning bolts correspond to the Lord's arrows and multiplied lightning flashes scattering opponents in the psalm.

relationship: narrative analogue for destructive divine hail
rationale: The hailstones hurled in fury recall the hail and fire that struck Egypt's people, livestock and vegetation; Exodus does not supply the catapult image.

relationship: parallel storm sweeping away rulers
rationale: Wisdom joins storm-driven destruction to overturned rulers' thrones; Isaiah likewise depicts rulers deprived of power and carried away like brushwood by a storm.

relationship: close address to kings and judges
rationale: Both directly summon kings to understand and those who judge the earth to receive instruction.

relationship: parallel instruction addressed to rulers
rationale: The rulers of multitudes are told to listen here; the psalm similarly tells kings to accept instruction and serve the Lord rather than face His anger.

relationship: parallel divine source and service of authority
rationale: Wisdom locates rulers' authority in the Lord and subjects their conduct to examination; Romans likewise derives authority from God and calls it His servant for good.

relationship: parallel rebuke of unjust judges
rationale: Wisdom indicts royal servants who judge wrongly; the psalm rebukes unjust judgment and demands protection of the poor and needy.

relationship: parallel greater accountability for privilege
rationale: Wisdom warns that high position receives severe judgment; Luke's servant teaching likewise requires more from those entrusted with more.

relationship: parallel unequal severity of examination
rationale: The contrast between pardon for the least and powerful examination of the mighty corresponds to differing blows and responsibility in Luke, without equating rank with knowledge.

relationship: parallel divine impartiality
rationale: The Master refuses deference to greatness; Romans likewise states that there is no partiality with God.

relationship: parallel accountability of those entrusted with much
rationale: The mighty face a forceful inquiry; Luke similarly says that those entrusted with much will be asked for more.

relationship: parallel wisdom's necessity for rulers
rationale: The call for rulers to learn wisdom corresponds to personified Wisdom's declaration that kings reign and rulers govern through her.

relationship: explicit same-chapter development of holy observance
rationale: The promise attached to holy observance and instruction is developed by the later link between keeping wisdom's laws and assurance of incorruption.

relationship: parallel desire for instructive words
rationale: The speaker urges longing for his words to gain instruction; Proverbs asks children to hear discipline and keep the teacher's utterance in their hearts.

relationship: close love-seek-find wisdom promise
rationale: Both promise that people who love and seek wisdom will find her.

relationship: parallel wisdom's initiative in making herself known
rationale: Wisdom goes ahead of those desiring her; Proverbs presents her publicly stationed at paths and gates, calling to humanity.

relationship: close vigilant-seeker and gate imagery
rationale: The early seeker finds wisdom beside his gates; Proverbs blesses the person who stays awake daily at her doors and entrances.

relationship: parallel reflection bringing freedom from fear
rationale: Reflection and vigilance for wisdom release care; Proverbs similarly connects keeping counsel and thought with confident walking and peaceful sleep.

relationship: parallel wisdom meeting people on their paths
rationale: Wisdom seeks worthy people and appears on their paths; Proverbs likewise locates her between paths and at entrances, addressing human beings.

relationship: related love and disciplined attachment to wisdom
rationale: Wisdom links desire for discipline with love; Proverbs joins loving wisdom to holding fast to discipline for one's life.

relationship: parallel love expressed in commandment keeping
rationale: Wisdom defines love through keeping her laws; Jesus likewise connects love for Him with keeping His commandments, in a different personal setting.

relationship: parallel wisdom leading to kingship
rationale: Wisdom says desire for her leads toward kingship; Proverbs states that kings reign through Wisdom.

relationship: related moral establishment of a throne
rationale: Rulers are urged to honor wisdom to reign enduringly; Proverbs similarly connects the establishment of a ruling throne with righteousness.

relationship: parallel disclosure of wisdom's beginning
rationale: The promised account of wisdom from her origin corresponds to Proverbs' extended speech about Wisdom's beginning and presence at creation.

relationship: parallel incompatibility of envy and true wisdom
rationale: The speaker refuses wasting envy because it has no share with wisdom; James likewise denies heavenly wisdom to bitter jealousy and contrasts it with pure, peaceable wisdom.

relationship: parallel communal safety through abundant counsel
rationale: The multitude of wise people safeguards the world here; Proverbs similarly locates deliverance in much counsel.

relationship: parallel beneficial instruction
rationale: The appeal to be instructed for one's benefit corresponds to a father's good gift of discipline and law to attentive children.

relationship: creation-from-earth background
rationale: The speaker traces his common mortality to the first earthborn man; Genesis narrates God's forming the human being from earth's dust.

relationship: narrative example of ordinary infant care
rationale: The royal speaker recalls swaddling and care; Luke likewise depicts the newborn Jesus wrapped in swaddling cloths, a shared concrete feature rather than proof of identical circumstances.

relationship: parallel common entrance and departure
rationale: Wisdom declares a common entrance to life and departure; Job likewise connects naked emergence from his mother's womb with naked departure.

relationship: parallel wisdom given in response to prayer
rationale: The speaker receives understanding when he prays; James similarly instructs anyone lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives it.

relationship: parallel wisdom preferred to wealth
rationale: The speaker reckons wealth as nothing beside wisdom; Proverbs likewise values her above gold, silver and costly stones.

relationship: close precious-metals and stones comparison
rationale: Both explicitly rank wisdom above gold, silver and costly stones, though Wisdom intensifies the comparison through sand and clay.

relationship: explicit same-chapter explanation of wisdom above light
rationale: Choosing wisdom over light because her radiance never sleeps is explained by her superiority to the sun and the failure of evil to overpower her.

relationship: close wealth-in-wisdom's-hand image
rationale: Good things and immeasurable wealth come with wisdom here; Proverbs likewise places wealth and glory in her left hand.

relationship: internal connection of wisdom and the goods she produces
rationale: Wisdom is called the mother and leader of the accompanying goods; the next chapter similarly describes her as richer than possessions because she works all things.

relationship: parallel wisdom free from deceit and envy
rationale: Learning without deceit and sharing without envy correspond to James's rejection of jealous falsehood and description of heavenly wisdom without hypocrisy.

relationship: related instruction and friendship with God
rationale: Wisdom's disciplined gifts commend people to God's friendship; Jesus likewise connects friendship with obeying His commands and receiving what He heard from the Father.

relationship: narrative analogue for divinely guided speech
rationale: The speaker asks God to guide his speech and reflection; God similarly promises Moses to open his mouth and teach what he should say.

relationship: close divine-hand dependence of the wise
rationale: Wisdom places people, words and understanding in God's hand; Ecclesiastes likewise puts the righteous, wise and their works in God's hand.

relationship: related divine wisdom and the ordered natural world
rationale: God-given knowledge of the world's composition corresponds to Job's depiction of God knowing wisdom and ordering winds, waters and rain.

relationship: creation background for knowledge of times
rationale: The knowledge of seasons and temporal divisions concerns the calendar that Genesis assigns to the heavenly lights for signs, seasons, days and years.

relationship: creation background for stellar and yearly order
rationale: Knowledge of yearly cycles and star positions corresponds to the lights and stars appointed in Genesis to govern temporal and celestial order.

relationship: Solomonic natural-knowledge parallel
rationale: Wisdom lists knowledge of creatures and plants; Kings likewise describes Solomon speaking about trees, livestock, birds, creeping things and fish, without supplying all the other fields listed here.

relationship: parallel wisdom's relation to all created works
rationale: Wisdom is the artisan of all things and the speaker's teacher; the psalm likewise attributes God's manifold works to wisdom.

relationship: related description of pure wisdom
rationale: Wisdom's intelligent, holy and undefiled spirit corresponds to James's description of heavenly wisdom as first pure and then morally beneficent; the lists are not identical.

relationship: internal expansion of wisdom's benevolent universal spirit
rationale: The spirit that loves humanity and oversees all develops the opening description of wisdom's human-loving spirit and the world-filling Spirit's knowledge.

relationship: internal parallel of wisdom's universal reach
rationale: Wisdom's penetration of all things corresponds to her mighty reach from end to end and governance of all things.

relationship: related divine-glory emanation imagery
rationale: Wisdom is a pure outflow of God's glory; Hebrews describes the Son as the radiance of His glory. The relationship concerns shared imagery, without claiming the verse explicitly identifies Wisdom as the Son.

relationship: close radiance-and-image imagery
rationale: Wisdom is radiance of eternal light and an image of divine goodness; Hebrews calls the Son radiance of glory and imprint of God's being, a literary-theological parallel with distinct formulations.

relationship: related renewal through divine spiritual agency
rationale: Wisdom renews all things while passing into holy souls; the psalm connects the sending of God's Spirit with creation and renewal of the earth, without supplying the prophet-making detail.

relationship: related divine love and faithful indwelling
rationale: God loves the one dwelling with wisdom; Jesus likewise promises the Father's love and divine dwelling to those keeping His word.

relationship: explicit same-chapter comparison of wisdom with light
rationale: Wisdom's superiority to sun, stars and light supplies the basis for the speaker's earlier choice of her over light.

relationship: related unconquered-light motif
rationale: Wisdom's superiority to alternating daylight is expressed as evil's failure to overpower her; John similarly says darkness did not overcome the light, with its own account of the Word.

relationship: internal parallel of universal ordered governance
rationale: Wisdom governs all things well from end to end; the later prayer describes God arranging all things by measure, number and weight.

relationship: related personification of wisdom as intimate companion
rationale: Wisdom is sought as a bride here; Proverbs asks the learner to call wisdom a sister and understanding a familiar companion, using different family images for close attachment.

relationship: parallel divine delight in companion wisdom
rationale: Wisdom's shared life with God and the Master's love correspond to Proverbs' Wisdom beside God as the one in whom He delighted.

relationship: parallel wisdom's participation in divine works
rationale: Wisdom knows God and His works here; Proverbs depicts her present beside Him as the heavens and earth are ordered.

relationship: parallel wisdom as source of richer possessions
rationale: Wisdom surpasses wealth because she works all things; Proverbs likewise associates her with wealth, righteousness and storehouses filled for those who love her.

relationship: related incomparable creative wisdom
rationale: Wisdom's unsurpassed skill corresponds to the wisdom by which God founded the earth and prepared the heavens.

relationship: parallel wisdom producing moral and governing virtues
rationale: Wisdom teaches self-control, understanding, righteousness and courage; Proverbs assigns her understanding, strength and righteous judgment, a related but not identical enumeration.

relationship: close wise understanding of riddles
rationale: Wisdom's understanding of turns of speech and solutions of riddles corresponds to the stated purpose of Proverbs: understanding obscure sayings and wise riddles.

relationship: parallel wisdom as counselor
rationale: The speaker chooses wisdom as counselor and encouragement; personified Wisdom in Proverbs likewise makes counsel her dwelling and possesses counsel and security.

relationship: parallel honor gained through wisdom
rationale: Wisdom brings the young speaker honor; Proverbs likewise promises that honoring her will bring exaltation and a crown of grace, without the same age contrast.

relationship: narrative example of admired wise judgment
rationale: The anticipated keenness in judgment corresponds to Israel's response to Solomon's judgment, recognizing God's discernment within him.

relationship: close silenced-listeners image
rationale: The speaker expects listeners to wait and place hands on their mouths; Job recalls powerful people stopping speech and putting a finger to their mouths before him.

relationship: parallel enduring remembrance of righteousness
rationale: Wisdom promises the speaker everlasting remembrance; the psalm likewise calls the righteous person an everlasting memorial.

relationship: parallel governance through wisdom
rationale: The speaker expects to govern peoples through wisdom; Proverbs explicitly declares that kings and sovereigns rule through her.

relationship: parallel peaceful companionship with wisdom
rationale: Life with wisdom brings gladness without bitterness or anguish; Proverbs similarly describes all her paths as peaceful.

relationship: internal wisdom-incorruption connection
rationale: The speaker finds immortality in kinship with wisdom; the earlier chain joins attention to her laws with incorruption and nearness to God.

relationship: parallel benefits of loving companionship with wisdom
rationale: The speaker seeks wisdom for delight, understanding and unfailing wealth; Proverbs likewise promises wealth and filled storehouses to those who love her.

relationship: close wisdom-as-prayed-for-gift parallel
rationale: Recognizing that God must give wisdom leads the speaker to petition Him; James similarly directs the person lacking wisdom to ask God for it.

relationship: close creation-by-divine-word motif
rationale: The prayer addresses the God who made all things by His word; the psalm likewise says the heavens were established by His word and creation followed His command.

relationship: close human-creation and dominion parallel
rationale: Wisdom describes humanity fashioned to rule God's creatures; Genesis likewise links creation in God's image with rule over earthly living things.

relationship: parallel righteous administration
rationale: The human vocation to govern in holiness and upright judgment corresponds to the royal prayer for righteous judgment and protection of the poor.

relationship: Solomonic prayer for wisdom parallel
rationale: The request for wisdom beside God's thrones recalls Solomon's request for a discerning heart and God's grant of wisdom for judgment.

relationship: close slave-and-slave-woman formula
rationale: Both prayers address the Lord as His slave and the son of His slave woman, though Wisdom adds frailty and deficient understanding.

relationship: related insufficiency of merely human wisdom
rationale: Human perfection without God's wisdom counts as nothing here; Paul likewise exposes worldly wisdom's inadequacy before God's wisdom, with his distinct focus on the crucified Christ.

relationship: Solomonic divine-election parallel
rationale: The speaker says God chose him as king and judge of His people; Chronicles likewise names God's choice of Solomon for the throne and divine sonship.

relationship: Solomonic temple-building commission
rationale: God's command to build the temple corresponds to Chronicles' explicit choice of Solomon to build God's house; the target does not supply the holy-tent comparison.

relationship: close wisdom-present-at-creation parallel
rationale: Wisdom is with God and present at world-making; Proverbs likewise depicts her beside Him during the establishment of heaven and earth.

relationship: parallel prayer for divinely given wisdom
rationale: The request that God send heavenly wisdom to guide action corresponds to James's instruction to ask God for wisdom.

relationship: parallel wisdom guarding and guiding conduct
rationale: Wisdom promises prudent guidance and protection; Proverbs likewise says wisdom entering the mind brings guarding counsel and rescue from an evil way.

relationship: Solomonic wisdom for righteous judgment
rationale: The speaker expects to judge God's people rightly through wisdom; Solomon likewise asks for discernment to judge the people in righteousness and receives a wise heart.

relationship: close question about knowing God's purpose
rationale: Wisdom asks who can know the Lord's will; Isaiah similarly asks who knew His mind or could instruct Him as counselor.

relationship: related limitation of unaided human understanding
rationale: Wisdom calls mortal reasoning uncertain; Paul describes the natural person's inability to receive what requires spiritual discernment, a related limitation in a different argument.

relationship: close bodily-tent and burden imagery
rationale: Wisdom portrays the earthly tent burdening the mind; Paul likewise describes those in the earthly tent groaning under its burden while awaiting life.

relationship: related contrast of earthly and heavenly knowledge
rationale: Wisdom contrasts difficult earthly inference with inaccessible heavenly inquiry; Jesus similarly contrasts failure concerning earthly things with difficulty receiving heavenly things.

relationship: close Spirit-given knowledge of God
rationale: God's purpose becomes known through wisdom and the Spirit sent from above; Paul likewise says the Spirit reveals what belongs to God and what He has freely given.

relationship: related salvation through divine wisdom
rationale: Wisdom concludes that people were saved through wisdom; Paul likewise joins God's wisdom to salvation, explicitly identifying Christ as God's wisdom in his own argument.

relationship: creation background of the first-formed father
rationale: The first-formed father recalls the human formed by God from earth; Genesis supplies that creation background but does not itself attribute deliverance from transgression to Wisdom.

relationship: close original-human dominion parallel
rationale: Wisdom's gift of strength to rule all things corresponds to God's commission that humanity subdue the earth and rule its creatures.

relationship: Cain narrative allusion
rationale: The angry brother-killer recalls Cain's distress and killing of Abel. Genesis does not narrate Cain's immediate death, so the source's perishing with passions is not treated as an identical narrative detail.

relationship: Noah-and-ark narrative allusion
rationale: The righteous man's rescue through humble wood recalls the timber ark and covenant of preservation given to Noah; Wisdom adds her guiding role.

relationship: Abraham's child-sacrifice test allusion
rationale: The righteous man's strength against compassion for his child corresponds to Abraham's binding of Isaac and refusal to withhold his beloved son; this target addresses that clause, not the earlier confused nations.

relationship: Lot's rescue from fiery destruction
rationale: The escaping righteous man recalls Lot being brought out before the Lord's fire overthrew the cities.

relationship: close salt-pillar and smoking-land allusion
rationale: The standing salt pillar and smoking wasteland recall Lot's wife becoming salt and Abraham seeing furnace-like vapor over the destroyed country; Genesis does not mention unripened plants.

relationship: parallel enduring warning from Sodom's destruction
rationale: Wisdom treats the destroyed region as a memorial of folly; Peter likewise calls Sodom and Gomorrah an example for future ungodly people.

relationship: parallel rescue of the godly from trouble
rationale: Wisdom rescues her servants after the Lot example; Peter similarly moves from Lot's rescue to the Lord's ability to rescue godly people from trial.

relationship: Jacob's guided flight and heavenly revelation
rationale: The fugitive shown divine realities recalls Jacob's dream of the heavenly ladder and God's promise to guard him on every road, after the brother's anger described in Genesis 27.

relationship: Jacob protected against exploitation
rationale: Wisdom's protection and enrichment of the exploited righteous man correspond to Jacob's account of Laban's cheating and God's transfer of livestock to him.

relationship: Jacob's contest and divine preservation
rationale: The mighty contest and discovery of the strength of devotion recall Jacob's wrestling, blessing, new name and declaration that his life was preserved after seeing God.

relationship: Joseph's refusal of sin
rationale: The sold righteous man rescued from sin recalls Joseph refusing his master's wife's demand because it would be evil before God.

relationship: Joseph's elevation after imprisonment
rationale: The movement from bonds to authority over rulers culminates in Pharaoh's recognition of Joseph's divine discernment and appointment over Egypt; the surrounding Genesis 39 narrative supplies the false accusation and imprisonment.

relationship: Israel's liberation from oppression
rationale: Wisdom's rescue of a holy people corresponds to the Lord's promise to free Israel from Egyptian slavery and take them as His people.

relationship: Moses opposing Pharaoh through signs
rationale: Wisdom's entrance into a servant and opposition to kings through wonders recalls Moses and Aaron's commission to confront Pharaoh with God's multiplied signs.

relationship: close cloud-and-fire guidance allusion
rationale: The covering by day and flame by night correspond to the cloud and fire pillars guiding Israel in Exodus.

relationship: Red Sea crossing allusion
rationale: Wisdom's guidance across the Red Sea corresponds to the opened sea and Israel's passage between walls of water.

relationship: Egyptian drowning and shore allusion
rationale: The overwhelmed enemies cast up from the depth correspond to the returning sea drowning Egypt's army and Israel seeing their bodies on the shore.

relationship: song after sea-deliverance allusion
rationale: The united hymn praising God's fighting hand corresponds to Moses and Israel singing of the drowned enemy and the Lord's victorious right hand.

relationship: close infants' mouths and divine praise motif
rationale: Wisdom enables infants' tongues to speak in the setting of praise; the psalm likewise attributes praise from infants' mouths to God.

relationship: parallel mediation through the Exodus prophet
rationale: Wisdom prospers the people's works by a holy prophet; Hosea similarly says the Lord brought Israel from Egypt and preserved him through a prophet.

relationship: wilderness-journey background
rationale: Travel through an uninhabited, trackless desert corresponds to the Lord's leading through the great, fearful and waterless wilderness.

relationship: narrative example of repelling desert enemies
rationale: The people's opposition to adversaries corresponds to Israel's battle with Amalek and Joshua's rout of the attackers.

relationship: close thirst-and-rock-water allusion
rationale: The thirsty people's appeal and water from rock correspond to the thirst at Rephidim, Moses's cry and the Lord's provision from Horeb's rock.

relationship: internal development of one creation serving opposite ends
rationale: The principle of enemies punished while Israel benefits is developed through harmful creatures for oppressors and quail as food for God's people.

relationship: river-turned-to-blood allusion
rationale: The ever-flowing river made bloody corresponds to the Nile water struck into blood, killing fish and becoming undrinkable.

relationship: background of the infant-killing decree
rationale: Wisdom interprets the water contrast as a rebuke for killing infants; Exodus supplies Pharaoh's orders to kill Hebrew boys and cast them into the river.

relationship: internal parallel of need as instruction
rationale: Israel's thirst teaches how opponents were punished; the later food contrast likewise says Israel's brief need showed how their enemies were tormented.

relationship: parallel merciful testing in the wilderness
rationale: Wisdom treats Israel's trials as discipline in mercy; Deuteronomy likewise explains wilderness deprivation as testing and fatherly instruction.

relationship: parallel fatherly divine discipline
rationale: The source distinguishes a father's instruction of Israel from a condemning king's judgment; Hebrews elaborates the fatherly side through God's beneficial discipline of sons.

relationship: internal recognition of God through contrasted rescue
rationale: Enemies recognize the Lord on hearing of benefits given to Israel; the later account similarly says rescue convinced enemies that God delivers from every evil.

relationship: Moses's final recognition in Egypt
rationale: The once exposed and rejected person later admired corresponds to Moses becoming great in the Egyptians' sight; his infancy is supplied by the separately read Exodus 2 context.

relationship: animal-plague narrative background
rationale: The punishment through irrational animals recalls frogs covering Egypt. Wisdom adds its interpretation as recompense for animal worship, which these Exodus verses do not state.

relationship: narrative example of punishment matching wrongdoing
rationale: Adoni-bezek explicitly recognizes his own mutilation as God's repayment for the same act he inflicted on others, illustrating Wisdom's matching-recompense principle.

relationship: related creation from an unformed condition
rationale: Wisdom appeals to God's creative power over unformed matter; Genesis describes the earth as unseen and unformed before the command for light, without resolving every philosophical implication of Wisdom's wording.

relationship: close measure-and-weight ordering imagery
rationale: God's arrangement by measure, number and weight corresponds to Isaiah's depiction of measured waters, spanned heaven and weighed mountains.

relationship: parallel irresistible divine strength
rationale: Wisdom asks who can oppose God's mighty arm; Job similarly asks who hardened himself against the mighty God and endured.

relationship: close drop-and-scale comparison
rationale: Wisdom compares the world with a slight tipping of scales and a dew drop; Isaiah likewise compares nations with a bucket's drop and a scale's slight tipping.

relationship: parallel mercy directed toward repentance
rationale: God overlooks sins with repentance in view; Romans likewise says divine kindness and forbearance lead people to repentance.

relationship: parallel kindness toward all God's works
rationale: God loves what He made here; the psalm likewise extends the Lord's kindness and compassion over all His works.

relationship: parallel creation's dependence on God's sustaining will
rationale: Wisdom asks how anything could endure without God's will; the psalm depicts creatures depending on His food, breath and renewing Spirit.

relationship: related divine ownership of the living world
rationale: Wisdom grounds God's sparing care in all things belonging to Him; the psalm likewise declares the earth, its fullness and inhabitants to be the Lord's.

relationship: internal parallel of the Spirit's universal presence
rationale: The incorruptible Spirit in all things corresponds to the opening declaration that the Lord's Spirit has filled the inhabited world.

relationship: parallel patient correction for repentance
rationale: Gradual reproof seeks release from evil and renewed belief; Romans similarly presents God's patient kindness as leading to repentance.

relationship: background of the land's former inhabitants
rationale: The introduction of the ancient inhabitants leads into their judgment; Deuteronomy likewise explains the removal of nations from the inherited land through their ungodliness.

relationship: close condemnation of sorcery and forbidden rites
rationale: Wisdom's detestable sorcery and rites correspond to Deuteronomy's prohibited divination, spells and practices that occasion the nations' removal.

relationship: parallel condemnation of ritual child-killing
rationale: Wisdom condemns murdered children in unholy ritual; the psalm likewise condemns sacrificing sons and daughters and shedding their innocent blood, without describing the flesh-eating detail.

relationship: background of destroyed nations and child sacrifice
rationale: Wisdom connects murderous parents with removal by Israel's ancestors; Deuteronomy likewise joins the nations' destruction with the abomination of burning children to their gods.

relationship: parallel land-transfer under divine promise
rationale: The land's reception of God's children corresponds to Israel inheriting the nations' land as God establishes the oath to the fathers; Deuteronomy cautions against claiming Israel's own righteousness as the cause.

relationship: close hornets and gradual expulsion allusion
rationale: Both describe hornets preceding Israel and the inhabitants being driven out little by little rather than all at once.

relationship: internal comparison of unused divine means
rationale: The ability to crush enemies by beasts or a stern word recalls the earlier hypothetical destructive creatures and single breath; neither passage claims these imagined beasts were actual plagues.

relationship: parallel delayed judgment as room for repentance
rationale: Gradual judgment gives time to repent despite ingrained evil; Romans similarly contrasts repentance under divine patience with an unrepentant heart storing up wrath.

relationship: close unanswerable-question formula
rationale: Both ask who could challenge God with the question, 'What hast Thou done?' when His action cannot be turned back.

relationship: parallel exclusive divine authority
rationale: Wisdom denies any rival god to whom the Lord must justify judgment; Deuteronomy likewise declares that no god stands beside Him and none can deliver from His hands.

relationship: parallel impotence of rulers before divine judgment
rationale: No king can confront God over His punishment here; the psalm likewise portrays assembled rulers facing divine laughter and anger.

relationship: close appeal to the justice of the universal Judge
rationale: Wisdom rejects condemning one undeserving of punishment; Abraham likewise appeals to the Judge of all earth not to destroy righteous and ungodly indiscriminately.

relationship: internal connection of power and mercy
rationale: Wisdom derives sparing mercy from universal mastery; the earlier prayer similarly grounds mercy toward all in God's ability to do all things.

relationship: narrative example of power displayed against defiance
rationale: God displays strength when His power is disbelieved; Exodus likewise interprets Pharaoh's preservation as an occasion to display God's strength amid continued refusal.

relationship: parallel patient and merciful divine governance
rationale: God judges gently with great forbearance; the psalm similarly describes Him as compassionate, merciful and long-suffering.

relationship: parallel divine mercy as a human ethical example
rationale: God's works teach the righteous to love humanity; Jesus likewise grounds love for enemies and human mercy in the Father's kindness and mercy.

relationship: parallel leniency offering release from evil
rationale: Wisdom says even enemies receive time and room to abandon evil; Romans likewise interprets divine patience as an invitation to repentance.

relationship: background of good promises sworn to the fathers
rationale: The special care for descendants of oath-receiving fathers recalls God's oath to Abraham promising multiplied offspring and blessing.

relationship: parallel merciful judgment modeled on God
rationale: Wisdom's discipline teaches people to consider goodness when judging and expect mercy when judged; Luke similarly connects the Father's mercy with human restraint in judgment and reciprocal measure.

relationship: internal recurrence of punishment through one's abominations
rationale: The ungodly are tormented through their own abominations, restating the earlier animal-worship contrast and principle that the instruments of sin become instruments of punishment.

relationship: close foolish exchange for animal images
rationale: Wisdom depicts people mistaking despised animals for gods; Romans likewise describes claimed wisdom becoming folly through exchanging divine glory for animal images.

relationship: parallel rejected patience followed by judgment
rationale: Failure to heed lighter reproof leads to full divine judgment; Romans similarly contrasts patient kindness with accumulated wrath for unrepentance.

relationship: narrative analogue for recognizing God through creatures
rationale: Wisdom interprets animal punishment as exposing false gods; Exodus depicts failed attempts to produce gnats followed by the magicians' recognition of God's finger, without all of Wisdom's interpretation.

relationship: close failure to know God from created works
rationale: Both fault people who fail to give God proper recognition despite the evidence of what He made.

relationship: parallel rejection of worshiping heavenly creation
rationale: Wisdom lists natural powers and heavenly lights falsely treated as gods; Deuteronomy expressly warns against worshiping sun, moon, stars and heaven's array.

relationship: related Creator's superiority to the heavens
rationale: Wisdom directs admiration beyond beautiful created things to their Maker; Isaiah likewise challenges comparisons with God and points to His authorship of the heavenly array.

relationship: parallel inference from cosmic power to its Maker
rationale: The power of created things should direct thought to their stronger Maker; Isaiah similarly attributes the ordered heavenly host to God's abundant might.

relationship: close knowledge of the unseen Maker through visible works
rationale: Wisdom says the Maker is seen by analogy from created greatness and beauty; Romans likewise says invisible divine qualities are understood through created things.

relationship: related searching for God
rationale: Wisdom grants that some mistaken people are seeking God; Acts likewise describes humanity seeking and feeling its way toward Him, without making the same judgment about their degree of blame.

relationship: parallel attention to creation displacing its Creator
rationale: The attractive appearance of God's works persuades people wrongly; Romans likewise criticizes reverence directed to creation instead of its Creator.

relationship: close denial of excuse
rationale: Both explicitly deny excuse to those who fail to recognize God in the setting of available evidence from creation.

relationship: parallel accountability for misused available knowledge
rationale: Wisdom questions extensive inquiry that misses the world's Master; Romans likewise treats available knowledge as grounds for accountability when God is not honored.

relationship: close handmade-metal-idol description
rationale: Both identify the nations' supposed gods as silver or gold and works of human hands.

relationship: parallel account of worked wood before idolatry
rationale: Both describe a craftsman's selecting and shaping wood within an argument that contrasts its ordinary human uses with its manufacture into a supposed god.

relationship: close wood-scraps cooking motif
rationale: The craftsman burns leftover wood and eats his fill; Isaiah likewise describes using part of the wood to bake bread, roast meat and become satisfied.

relationship: close leftover-wood idol motif
rationale: Both portray the remainder of useful or burned wood being fashioned into a humanly made god.

relationship: internal recurrence of attractively painted idols
rationale: The image's applied red color and concealed blemishes correspond to the later colored, painted form that stirs foolish desire despite being lifeless.

relationship: close fastening an idol to prevent movement
rationale: The image is set in a wall and secured with iron; Jeremiah likewise describes idols fastened with hammers and nails so they do not move.

relationship: parallel dependence and helplessness of idols
rationale: The maker must stop his image falling because it cannot help itself; Jeremiah similarly presents fastened images that must be carried and cannot provide good.

relationship: close petition to a self-made god
rationale: The maker addresses a lifeless image for personal welfare; Isaiah likewise depicts the craftsman praying for rescue to the remainder he made into a god.

relationship: parallel inability of an idol to supply living action
rationale: Wisdom mocks petitions for life and travel to a dead, immobile object; the psalm likewise lists idols' unusable senses and feet that do not walk.

relationship: parallel useless objects asked to provide benefit
rationale: Wisdom exposes the powerless idol asked for successful work; Isaiah likewise calls manufactured gods useless and unable to help their makers.

relationship: contrast in maritime trust
rationale: Wisdom mocks a sailor's appeal to rotten wood; the psalm instead portrays endangered sailors calling to the Lord, who quiets the waves and guides them to harbor.

relationship: internal recurrence of wisdom as artisan
rationale: The ship is fashioned through wisdom the artisan; the earlier passage likewise calls wisdom the artisan of all things.

relationship: close path-through-the-sea formula
rationale: God's providence provides a way in the sea and safe path among waves, closely recalling Isaiah's description of the Lord making a path in strong water.

relationship: parallel divine rescue from maritime danger
rationale: Wisdom celebrates salvation even when the traveler lacks skill; the psalm likewise makes rescue depend on the Lord's response and guidance when sailors' wisdom has failed.

relationship: ark background for preservation through wood
rationale: The argument about life entrusted to wood leads directly to the flood example; Genesis narrates the floating ark and the preservation of Noah and its occupants amid destruction.

relationship: Noah's preservation as hope for continued life
rationale: Wisdom's surviving seed on a raft recalls Noah and the ark's occupants remaining after the flood; the giants belong to the separately read Genesis 6 setting.

relationship: ark-context explanation of blessed wood
rationale: The blessed wood follows the flood rescue and corresponds to Noah's commanded timber ark and promised preservation; this link does not assert an explicit reference to the cross.

relationship: parallel condemnation of fabricated idols and attachment to them
rationale: Wisdom condemns the handmade god and maker; Deuteronomy calls the carved image an abomination and warns that its possessor can become subject to its ban.

relationship: parallel divine rejection of wickedness and its practitioners
rationale: Wisdom joins God's hatred of ungodliness and the ungodly person; the psalm likewise says God hates workers of lawlessness and abhors the deceitful, bloodthirsty person.

relationship: parallel joined judgment of idol and human participant
rationale: The deed and doer receive punishment together; Deuteronomy similarly warns that bringing an abominable image home can bring its ban upon the person.

relationship: close idol-as-stumbling-block image
rationale: Wisdom calls idols stumbling blocks and snares for souls; the psalm likewise says service to carved images became a stumbling block.

relationship: parallel idolatry leading to sexual impurity
rationale: Wisdom connects invented idols with sexual immorality; Romans likewise moves from exchanged divine glory to bodily impurity in disordered desires.

relationship: parallel impermanence of false gods
rationale: Wisdom denies that idols will endure forever; Jeremiah similarly calls for gods that did not create heaven and earth to perish.

relationship: parallel end appointed for fabricated gods
rationale: The idols' vainglorious invention is assigned an end; Jeremiah likewise calls fabricated images false and destined to perish at visitation.

relationship: narrative example of ruler-commanded image worship
rationale: Wisdom describes carved images worshiped by royal command; Daniel supplies a concrete case of commanded worship, without identifying the golden image as a portrait of the king.

relationship: related artistic production of ideal human beauty
rationale: Wisdom describes a likeness made more beautiful by artistic effort; Isaiah likewise describes an idol made in human form and beauty, without the same royal-flattery motive.

relationship: parallel human likeness promoted to worship
rationale: Wisdom describes a previously honored human becoming an object of worship; Romans likewise condemns replacing divine glory with a corruptible human image.

relationship: parallel exclusivity of the divine name and honor
rationale: Wisdom condemns giving wood and stone the unshared name; Isaiah likewise declares the Lord's name and refusal to give His glory or praiseworthy deeds to carved images.

relationship: parallel false declaration of peace amid evil
rationale: Wisdom criticizes calling grave evils peace; Jeremiah similarly exposes dishonest people who proclaim peace while treating the people's fracture with contempt.

relationship: parallel condemnation of child-killing rites
rationale: Wisdom condemns rites that murder children; Deuteronomy likewise calls burning children to gods an abomination the Lord hates.

relationship: parallel collapse of life and marital fidelity
rationale: Wisdom pairs murder with adultery amid ignorance of God; Hosea likewise joins lack of divine recognition with murder, adultery and bloodshed.

relationship: close catalogue of violence, theft and deception
rationale: The disorderly catalogue of murder, theft and deceit corresponds to Hosea's linked cursing, falsehood, murder, theft and adultery.

relationship: related catalogue of moral and relational disorder
rationale: Both accounts connect rejected knowledge of God with disturbed relations, dishonor, faithlessness and broader moral disorder; their lists are not identical.

relationship: parallel connection of idolatry with proliferating wrongdoing
rationale: Wisdom calls idol worship the source of evil; Romans similarly develops a sequence from exchanged worship to impurity and numerous injustices.

relationship: related accountability for false oaths
rationale: Among the corrupt practices Wisdom names is ready false swearing; Zechariah expressly depicts judgment entering the false swearer's house.

relationship: related swearing by non-gods
rationale: Wisdom exposes people who trust lifeless idols when swearing wrongly; Jeremiah likewise condemns swearing by those who are not gods.

relationship: parallel judgment pursuing false swearing
rationale: Wisdom promises consequences for deceitful oaths despite the idols' helplessness; Zechariah likewise sends divine judgment into the false swearer's house.

relationship: parallel divine justice behind oath judgment
rationale: Wisdom locates punishment in justice rather than the power of the named idols; Zechariah explicitly makes the Lord the sender of judgment against false swearing.

relationship: close description of God's patient mercy
rationale: Both address God as patient, merciful and true, grounding trust in His character.

relationship: related rejection of sin as a response to grace
rationale: Wisdom's acknowledgment of belonging to God even amid sin does not endorse continued sin; Paul likewise rejects continuing in sin so that grace may increase.

relationship: close knowledge-of-God and eternal-life association
rationale: Wisdom calls knowledge of God the root of immortality; Jesus likewise describes eternal life in terms of knowing the true God and the One He sent.

relationship: related resistance to manufactured likenesses
rationale: Wisdom says human inventions and painted forms did not mislead God's people; Deuteronomy likewise warns against turning the unseen God into a manufactured likeness.

relationship: internal contrast of attractive finish and lifelessness
rationale: The desired, colored image has no breath; the earlier portrait likewise describes an image painted attractively yet incapable of giving life or movement.

relationship: parallel joined assessment of idol-makers and worshipers
rationale: Wisdom joins the makers, desirers and worshipers in blame; the psalm likewise joins makers and those trusting idols in their fate.

relationship: close potter and differing-vessels analogy
rationale: Both describe a potter making vessels for differing uses from the same material; Wisdom discusses clean and opposite uses, while Romans speaks of honor and dishonor within an analogy about God.

relationship: close earth-origin and earth-return formula
rationale: The mortal potter will return to the earth from which he was taken, closely recalling the sentence that humanity is earth and returns to earth.

relationship: parallel rivalry driving skilled labor
rationale: The potter competes with metalworkers and prizes his imitations; Ecclesiastes likewise identifies rivalry with one's companion within toil and courage in work.

relationship: close ashes-heart criticism of idol-making
rationale: Wisdom calls the idol-maker's heart ashes; Isaiah likewise says the heart of those manufacturing and worshiping idols is ashes.

relationship: close divine-breath creation allusion
rationale: The unknown true Maker breathes an active soul and life-giving spirit into the person; Genesis likewise narrates God's breath of life and the human becoming a living soul.

relationship: related commercial pride about brief human life
rationale: Wisdom condemns reducing existence to a profitable fair; James likewise rebukes confident plans to trade and profit while ignoring life's vapor-like brevity and God's will.

relationship: internal recurrence of infant-like religious folly
rationale: The oppressors are judged more wretched than an infant's soul; the earlier passage likewise describes animal-worshipers as deceived like senseless infants.

relationship: close catalogue of idols' unusable senses
rationale: Both list idols' eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet while denying their ability to see, hear, perceive or walk.

relationship: contrast of borrowed life with the life-giving Creator
rationale: Wisdom contrasts a spirit-borrowing human maker with true divinity; Acts likewise says God gives life and breath and cannot be equated with a humanly formed image.

relationship: parallel lifelessness of manufactured gods
rationale: Wisdom distinguishes living mortal makers from their dead products; Jeremiah likewise says fabricated images are false and have no spirit in them.

relationship: parallel animal-directed idolatry
rationale: Wisdom condemns worship of irrational animals; Romans similarly describes the exchange of divine glory for images of birds, quadrupeds and creeping things.

relationship: contrast in evaluation of animals
rationale: Wisdom denies praise and blessing to the animals treated as gods; Genesis calls the created animals good. The comparison preserves these different evaluations rather than assuming identical objects of praise.

relationship: animal-plague narrative background
rationale: The oppressors' torment through beasts corresponds to the threatened dog-flies in Egyptian homes, contrasted with Israel's protection in Goshen.

relationship: quail-provision narrative allusion
rationale: Wisdom's beneficial quail food corresponds to the Lord's promise of meat and the quail covering Israel's camp.

relationship: internal contrast of punitive creatures and desired food
rationale: The contrast between repellent creatures and quail nourishment is recalled later through the production of gnats and frogs alongside quail satisfying the people's desire.

relationship: internal distinction of instructional trial and hostile judgment
rationale: Israel's brief lack shows how enemies are tormented; the earlier account likewise says merciful testing taught Israel how the ungodly suffered judgment.

relationship: serpent-plague and remedy allusion
rationale: The deadly snake attack followed by limited wrath corresponds to the serpents' bites and the remedy God gave through Moses.

relationship: salvation-symbol narrative allusion
rationale: The short admonition's visible symbol recalls the serpent placed on a standard at God's command, toward which the bitten could look and live.

relationship: interpretation of the serpent remedy
rationale: Wisdom attributes rescue to God rather than the visible object; Numbers supplies the commanded looking and resulting life, while Wisdom states the theological explanation.

relationship: parallel confidence in rescue from every evil
rationale: The source names God as the One rescuing from every evil; Paul likewise expresses confidence that the Lord will rescue him from every evil work.

relationship: related destructive-insect plague tradition
rationale: Wisdom describes fatal insect bites; the psalm likewise says a dog-fly devoured the Egyptians and locusts received their labors. It supports destructive insect judgment without specifying Wisdom's full account of fatal locust bites.

relationship: serpent-remedy and survival allusion
rationale: The serpents fail to overcome God's sons because mercy heals them; Numbers likewise reports bitten people looking at the bronze serpent and living.

relationship: narrative basis for remedial serpent discipline
rationale: The bites lead to renewed attention and rescue; Numbers similarly records confession, Moses's prayer and obedience to God's remedy, without explicitly stating Wisdom's warning about future forgetfulness.

relationship: close divine-word healing motif
rationale: Wisdom locates healing in God's word rather than a medicine; the psalm likewise says God sent His word, healed the afflicted and rescued them.

relationship: close life-death and Hades authority formula
rationale: Both declare God's power to put to death or give life and to bring down to Hades and bring up again.

relationship: parallel human inability to control death and spirit
rationale: Wisdom denies human ability to restore a departed spirit; Ecclesiastes similarly denies human authority to restrain the spirit or govern the day of death.

relationship: close inescapable-divine-hand formula
rationale: Wisdom says escape from God's hand is impossible; Deuteronomy likewise declares that none can deliver out of His hands.

relationship: hail-and-fire plague allusion
rationale: The ungodly pursued by hail, showers and fire recall the thunder, hail and fire that devastated Egypt's people and produce.

relationship: interpretation of fire amid hail
rationale: Wisdom marvels at fire operating in water; Exodus supplies the fire flaming amid hail, without explicitly explaining it as fire exceeding its natural power.

relationship: internal recurrence of fire sparing living creatures
rationale: The tamed flame that does not consume the punitive animals is recalled in the final account of flames not withering perishable animals walking among them.

relationship: plague destruction of produce
rationale: The fire that destroys the unrighteous land's produce belongs to the plague whose hail struck Egypt's plants and shattered its trees.

relationship: close heavenly and angelic bread description
rationale: Wisdom calls the provided food angels' food and bread from heaven; the psalm likewise calls manna heaven's bread and angels' bread.

relationship: manna-taste narrative background
rationale: Wisdom expands the nourishing food's sweetness into adaptation to each desired taste; Exodus describes manna's honey-cake taste but not that transformation.

relationship: fire-and-hail background of the paradox
rationale: Wisdom interprets enduring ice and snow beside destructive fire; Exodus reports fire flaming amid hail, without spelling out the same physical explanation.

relationship: internal recurrence of fire sparing heavenly food
rationale: The fire forgets its destructive power so that the righteous may be nourished; this corresponds to the final statement that flames did not wither the meltable heavenly food.

relationship: parallel creation obeying its Maker
rationale: Wisdom describes creation adjusting to God's purposes; the psalm likewise names fire, hail, snow, ice and storm wind as fulfilling His word.

relationship: internal account of creation's adaptable service
rationale: The nourishing gift is served by creation changing into all things; the concluding account describes elements being rearranged through an analogy with changing harp notes.

relationship: close nourishment-by-divine-utterance teaching
rationale: Wisdom interprets the food as teaching that God's utterance preserves humanity; Deuteronomy likewise interprets manna as teaching life by every word from God's mouth rather than bread alone.

relationship: close manna-melting-in-sunlight allusion
rationale: The heavenly food melts under a ray of sun; Exodus likewise says the gathered manna melted when the sun grew hot.

relationship: parallel early appeal to God
rationale: Wisdom draws a lesson of thanksgiving before sunrise; the psalm likewise addresses God in a rising-at-dawn appeal of longing.

relationship: internal comparison of failed hope to frost
rationale: The ungrateful person's hope melts like frost; the earlier passage likewise compares ungodly hope to fine frost driven by a storm, with a different mode of disappearance.

relationship: close immeasurable-divine-judgments motif
rationale: Wisdom calls God's judgments great and hard to recount; Paul likewise calls His judgments unsearchable and His ways untraceable.

relationship: darkness-plague narrative allusion
rationale: The oppressors' confinement in a long night corresponds to Egypt's three days of darkness, when people could not see one another or rise from bed.

relationship: contrast of attempted concealment and divine vision
rationale: The lawless imagine darkness can hide secret sins; the psalm instead declares that darkness does not conceal anything from God.

relationship: expanded description of Egypt's darkness
rationale: The failure of ordinary lights elaborates the narrative of tangible darkness over Egypt; Exodus records the darkness but not the separate failure of fire and stars.

relationship: related exposure of Egyptian magic's limits
rationale: Wisdom describes magical claims collapsing; Exodus supplies the magicians' failure to produce gnats and acknowledgment of God's finger, a related episode rather than an assertion that it occurred during the darkness.

relationship: parallel disproportionate terror under judgment
rationale: Wisdom depicts people trembling at passing animals and hissing; Leviticus likewise depicts cowardice in which a wind-blown leaf's sound provokes flight without a pursuer.

relationship: parallel accusing conscience
rationale: Wickedness condemns itself through conscience here; Romans likewise speaks of conscience bearing witness and inner reasonings accusing before God's judgment.

relationship: darkness-plague background of helpless rest
rationale: The common helpless night recalls Egypt's darkness and inability to rise from bed; Wisdom's description of its origin in Hades goes beyond Exodus's narration.

relationship: related frightening nocturnal experience
rationale: Wisdom describes apparitions and sudden paralyzing fear; Eliphaz likewise recounts nocturnal terrors, trembling and an unrecognized spiritual presence, in a different setting.

relationship: parallel confinement without physical bonds
rationale: The person becomes a prisoner without iron bars; Exodus similarly describes the darkness preventing people from rising from their beds.

relationship: parallel comprehensive restraint by darkness
rationale: Wisdom's workers of every occupation share one chain of darkness; Exodus likewise reports general Egyptian darkness and immobility, without enumerating occupations.

relationship: related sounds provoking fearful flight
rationale: The wind, birds, water and rocks belong to Wisdom's catalogue of terror-producing sounds; Leviticus likewise makes the sound of a moving leaf occasion cowardly flight.

relationship: parallel fear exceeding any pursuing enemy
rationale: Unseen movement, roars and echoes paralyze the people; Leviticus similarly describes flight and collapse even though no enemy pursues.

relationship: contrast between darkness's victims and those in light
rationale: Wisdom contrasts the afflicted region with the illuminated world; Exodus likewise contrasts Egyptian darkness with light where Israel lived, without making the broader worldwide statement.

relationship: Egyptian darkness interpreted as judgment
rationale: The heavy night over the oppressors alone develops Exodus's contrast between Egypt's darkness and Israel's light; Wisdom adds its image of future darkness and inward burden.

relationship: close light-for-Israel contrast
rationale: The holy ones' great light corresponds to Israel having light where they lived while Egyptians could not see one another.

relationship: ethical parallel of refusing retaliation
rationale: The previously injured holy ones do not harm their opponents; Paul likewise commands no repayment of evil for evil and overcoming evil with good.

relationship: fire-pillar guidance allusion
rationale: The blazing pillar guiding the unknown journey corresponds to the fire pillar by which God led Israel at night.

relationship: related worldwide mission of Israel's law
rationale: Wisdom says the sons kept captive were to mediate law's light to the world; Isaiah likewise depicts nations seeking instruction as law goes out from Zion.

relationship: background of the planned destruction of Hebrew infants
rationale: Wisdom interprets the later Egyptian deaths against the plan to kill Israel's infants; Exodus supplies Pharaoh's command to cast the Hebrew boys into the river.

relationship: patriarchal promise behind expected deliverance
rationale: Wisdom recalls ancestral assurance before the saving night; Genesis records the prior covenant announcement of foreign oppression, judgment upon the oppressing nation and the descendants' departure, without naming Passover's date.

relationship: Passover expectation of judgment and protection
