rationale: The people await the salvation of the righteous and enemies' destruction; Exodus announces the same night's striking of Egypt and sheltering of marked Israelite houses.

relationship: one event bringing judgment and protection
rationale: Wisdom's punishment of opponents and glorification of God's people correspond to the Passover night that strikes Egypt while preventing destruction in Israel's houses.

relationship: communal Passover-sacrifice background
rationale: The holy families' united sacrifice recalls the household allocation and whole congregation's slaughter of the Passover animal; Exodus does not supply the same account of ancestral hymns.

relationship: close Egyptian cry after firstborn deaths
rationale: Wisdom's pitiful mourning cry corresponds to the great cry through Egypt because every household had a dead person.

relationship: close judgment across social ranks
rationale: Wisdom joins slave, master, commoner and king in one judgment; Exodus likewise ranges from Pharaoh's firstborn to the captive woman's firstborn.

relationship: firstborn-death narrative background
rationale: The simultaneous loss of honored offspring corresponds to the midnight striking and widespread bereavement; Wisdom adds the claim that survivors could not bury all the dead.

relationship: close Israel-as-son and firstborn-judgment connection
rationale: Wisdom ties recognition of God's son to the firstborn's destruction; Exodus already links Israel as God's firstborn son with the threatened death of Pharaoh's firstborn.

relationship: midnight-judgment allusion
rationale: Wisdom's silence halfway through the night sets the judgment scene that Exodus explicitly locates at midnight.

relationship: related divine-word and sword imagery
rationale: Wisdom portrays God's commanded judgment through an armed, sword-bearing word; Hebrews likewise likens God's active, judging word to a penetrating sword, without identifying this Egyptian judgment as the incarnation.

relationship: firstborn judgment behind the cosmic-warrior image
rationale: The word filling the land with death interprets the Lord's midnight striking of Egypt; Exodus does not narrate the heaven-touching warrior's stature.

relationship: Israelite outbreak and halted wrath allusion
rationale: The righteous people's brief death trial recalls the outbreak among Israel that ceased after priestly atonement.

relationship: Aaron's incense intercession allusion
rationale: The minister hastening with incense to oppose wrath recalls Aaron running into the congregation with the fire pan and making atonement.

relationship: related intercession invoking the fathers' promises
rationale: The priestly appeal to ancestral oaths parallels Moses's distinct intercession recalling God's oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; the two mediators and episodes are not conflated.

relationship: close standing-between-dead-and-living allusion
rationale: Wisdom's mediator stands between the fallen and the living and checks wrath; Numbers explicitly says Aaron stood between dead and living and the outbreak subsided.

relationship: priestly four-row stones background
rationale: The fathers' glories engraved in four rows correspond to the breastpiece's four rows of stones bearing Israel's tribal names; Wisdom supplies its larger cosmic interpretation of the garment.

relationship: halted-outbreak narrative conclusion
rationale: The destroyer's yielding corresponds to the outbreak subsiding after Aaron's intercession; Numbers does not itself attribute this to fear of the priestly ornaments.

relationship: renewed Egyptian pursuit under divine judgment
rationale: The final fury anticipates the known pursuit; Exodus depicts Pharaoh's hardened heart and renewed pursuit after Israel had departed.

relationship: close change-of-heart and pursuit allusion
rationale: Both recount Egypt reversing its release of Israel and pursuing the departing people.

relationship: background of mourning and urgent expulsion
rationale: Wisdom stresses the folly of pursuing those just begged to leave; Exodus supplies the mourning cry and urgent Egyptian demand for Israel's departure before the subsequent pursuit.

relationship: parallel divine purpose in the final pursuit
rationale: Wisdom interprets the compulsion toward further punishment; Exodus likewise places the Egyptians' renewed entry into danger within God's announced purpose to display His glory, without mentioning forgetfulness.

relationship: close contrasting outcomes at the sea
rationale: The people's astonishing passage and enemies' death correspond to Israel walking on dry ground while the returning sea covers Egypt's forces.

relationship: creation background for the sea-crossing renewal image
rationale: Wisdom calls the elements' service a new fashioning of creation; Genesis's appearance of dry land from gathered water supplies the original creation pattern behind that comparison.

relationship: dry-road-through-the-sea allusion
rationale: Wisdom's dry way out of the sea corresponds to the divided waters and dry ground of Israel's crossing; the grass-bearing plain is Wisdom's additional description.

relationship: collective passage under God's protecting hand
rationale: The sheltered nation passes after seeing wonders; Exodus likewise describes Israel's safe passage and recognition of the Lord's great hand.

relationship: close horse-like Exodus guidance image
rationale: Wisdom likens the rescued people to grazing horses; Isaiah likewise compares God's guidance through the abyss to a horse in the wilderness and livestock on a plain, without the same leaping-lamb image.

relationship: close frogs-from-water and gnats-from-earth allusions
rationale: Wisdom recalls abnormal production of frogs from the river and gnats from earth; Exodus describes both the frogs rising from Egypt's waters and the dust becoming gnats.

relationship: background of desire for richer food
rationale: The request for luxurious foods recalls the people's intense craving for meat and dissatisfaction with manna.

relationship: close quail-from-the-sea allusion
rationale: Wisdom's quail coming from the sea correspond to the wind carrying quail across from the sea into Israel's camp.

relationship: earlier storm-signs background
rationale: The remembered violent thunderbolts correspond to the thunder, hail and fire that earlier struck Egypt; the target does not itself state Wisdom's comparative judgment about hostility to strangers.

relationship: background of the later enslavement of benefactors
rationale: The latter group enslaving formerly beneficial strangers corresponds to the new Pharaoh who did not know Joseph and Egypt's oppression of Israel. The former hostile hosts remain the distinct Sodom example.

relationship: judgment on the former hostile hosts
rationale: The announced visitation on the former group corresponds to Sodom's overthrow after the hostile treatment of visitors narrated earlier in Genesis 19, not to Egypt's later enslavement.

relationship: contrast between initial welcome and later oppression
rationale: Wisdom recalls that the later enslavers had first received Israel favorably; Genesis supplies Pharaoh's invitation to settle Jacob's family in the best land, before Exodus's oppressive labors.

relationship: close blindness-and-doorway comparison
rationale: Wisdom explicitly compares the later darkness with the men at the righteous person's doors; Genesis reports the Sodomites' blindness and inability to find Lot's door.

relationship: internal explanation of creation's altered service
rationale: The rearranged elements recapitulate creation stretching or relaxing to serve God's purposes and changing to provide His nourishing gift.

relationship: hail-fire narrative basis for reversed elemental behavior
rationale: Wisdom says fire exceeds its power in water; Exodus supplies the concrete combination of fire flaming amid hail, without describing the same change of natural properties.

relationship: internal recapitulation of restrained fire
rationale: The spared animals and meltable heavenly food summarize the earlier account of flame withheld from creatures and fire forgetting its power for Israel's nourishment.

relationship: parallel summary of sustained Exodus care
rationale: Wisdom concludes with God's continual support of His people; the psalm similarly summarizes their guidance as a flock through the wilderness, safety from the sea and arrival at their inheritance.
